svg.aria-label: Diagram: what a GuardDuty finding's severity encodes, and what a suppression rule actually removes. Each finding has a severity value anywhere in the 1.0 to 10.0 range reflecting the potential risk that finding could have to the environment, as determined by AWS security engineers, and GuardDuty divides the range into four bands. Low is 1.0 to 3.9 and indicates attempted suspicious activity that did not compromise the environment, for example a port scan or a failed intrusion attempt, with no immediate recommended action though it may indicate someone is looking for weak points. Medium is 4.0 to 6.9 and indicates suspicious activity deviating from normally observed behaviour that may be indicative of a resource compromise, with a recommendation to investigate at the earliest convenience and to consider the resource compromised if the activity cannot be confirmed as authorised. High is 7.0 to 8.9 and indicates the resource in question is compromised and actively being used for unauthorized purposes. Critical is 9.0 to 10.0 and indicates an attack sequence may be in progress or recently happened, and GuardDuty recommends prioritising triage and remediation of all critical findings because they can be part of a ransomware attack and can escalate at any time. A key qualifier is that a finding of a particular type may have a different severity depending on the context specific to the finding, so severity is a property of the occurrence rather than of the type. The central warning records the inversion: critical severity is defined in terms of an attack sequence, attack sequences are correlated from other findings, and AWS states that findings archived because of suppression rules are not considered as signals for attack sequences, that Extended Threat Detection cannot use archived findings when correlating events, and that broad suppression rules might impact the ability to detect multi-stage attacks. The worked example given is that a rule archiving all EKS cluster-related findings instead of targeting specific known activities prevents GuardDuty detecting an attack sequence where a threat actor exploits a container, obtains privileged tokens and accesses sensitive resources. A panel lists everything a suppression rule removes a finding from: Security Hub CSPM, Amazon S3, Amazon Detective and Amazon EventBridge, and if Malware Protection for EC2 is enabled the suppressed findings will not initiate a malware scan; the finding is still generated but marked archived and retained in GuardDuty for ninety days, viewable through ListFindings with a findingCriteria criterion of service.archived equal to true. A mechanism panel notes that in the API a filter and a suppression rule are the same object differing in one field, because the CreateFilter action parameter takes NOOP or ARCHIVE and defaults to NOOP, that the maximum number of saved filters per account per Region is one hundred, that the rank parameter from one to one hundred sets both the filter's position and the order in which it is applied, and that severity filter criteria are expressed as integers rather than decimals, with Low as one two three, Medium as four five six, High as seven eight, and Critical as nine ten. A closing panel records AWS's guidance to build suppression rules reactively and only for findings for which false positives have repeatedly been identified, the point being that a rule written before the behaviour has been seen has no evidence behind it rather than that it must be broadly scoped, since GuardDuty accepts the same granular criteria whenever a rule is created, to keep rules focused on specific behaviours, that only the GuardDuty administrator can create suppression rules in a multi-account environment, and that every documented example pairs a finding type with a second criterion identifying the legitimate cause: an on-premises egress gateway IP for instance credential exfiltration, a bastion host image or tag for SSH brute force, the vulnerability scanner's instances for port scans, and the Kubernetes DNS server pod's executable path or SHA-256 for duplicate DNS findings, since each pod lookup produces two DNS events.
svg.title: Severity describes one finding; the critical band describes several, correlated
svg.text: Severity rates one finding alone. Suppression removes it from the correlation too.
“the potential risk the finding could have to your environment” — anywhere in 1.0 to 10.0
Critical 9.0 – 10.0
“an attack sequence may be in progress or had recently happened”
prioritise all of them — “can be a part of a ransomware attack and can escalate at any time”
“the resource in question… is compromised and is actively being used for unauthorized purposes”
immediate remediation
Medium 4.0 – 6.9
“suspicious activity that deviates from normally observed behavior”
investigate soon; if you cannot confirm it was authorised, “consider the resource compromised”
“attempted suspicious activity that did not compromise your environment” — a port scan
“no immediate recommended action” → which is why these get a suppression rule
And the qualifier under all four: “A finding of a particular type may have a different severity depending on the context.”
Severity is a property of the occurrence, not of the type — so a runbook keyed on finding type is keyed on the wrong thing.
The inversion: the band you must prioritise is built from the band you suppress
Critical is defined as an attack sequence. An attack sequence is correlated from other findings. And:
“Findings that are archived because of suppression rules are not considered as signals for attack sequences.”
“Broad suppression rules might impact the ability of GuardDuty to detect behaviors aligned with… multi-stage attacks.”
AWS’s example: archive all EKS findings and it cannot detect “a threat actor exploits a container, obtains privileged
tokens, and accesses sensitive resources”.
What a suppression rule removes it from
Security Hub CSPM · Amazon S3 · Detective · EventBridge
+ Malware Protection for EC2: suppressed findings
“won’t initiate a malware scan”
+ attack-sequence correlation (above)
Still generated, marked archived, kept 90 days:
ListFindings · service.archived = true
A filter and a suppression rule differ by one field
action: NOOP | ARCHIVE Default: NOOP
NOOP = a saved view. ARCHIVE = detection config.
100 saved filters per account per Region
rank 1–100 sets the order filters are applied in
severity criteria are integers, not the decimal value:
Every documented example pairs a finding type with a second criterion naming the legitimate cause
InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS + API caller IPv4 of your on-premises egress gateway
EC2/SSHBruteForce + the image ID or tag of your bastion hosts
Recon:EC2/Portscan + the instances “that host these vulnerability assessment tools”
DNS findings + the coredns pod’s executablePath or executableSha256 — each pod lookup makes two DNS events
Never the finding type alone. The second criterion is what leaves the type live everywhere else.
AWS’s guidance, marked Important: build rules “reactively” and “only for findings for which you have repeatedly
identified false positives” — because a rule written before you have seen the behaviour has no evidence behind it.
In an organisation, “only the GuardDuty administrator can create suppression rules” — so the context and the decision sit apart.
Triage has two outputs. “Should a human look now?” is severity. “Should the detector stop seeing this?” is not.
The suppression rule answers the second while appearing to answer the first.
